title: Ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine
summary: A pit latrine with a dark cubicle and a screened vent pipe that draws smells up and out and traps flies. Dug deep, it is designed to last a household ten years or more with no water or power. The dangers are a pit wall collapsing on the digger, waste reaching a well when it's sited badly, and children falling in; it also works poorly in deep cold.

materials.item: Lining for at least the top 0.5–1 m: blocks, bricks or stone laid in mortar; more blockwork with open joints, or sandbags, lower down in loose soil
Old drums as a thin lining, only with a concrete ring beam on top
Cement, sand and gravel for mortar and the slab, plus steel bar or mesh for the slab
Heavy timbers or planks for a wooden slab, or for spreading the slab's load
Smooth plastic vent pipe, 150 mm (6 in) inside or larger, long enough to stand 0.5 m above the roof
Fly screen, 1.2 × 1.5 mm mesh: PVC-coated glass fibre, aluminium or stainless
materials.qty: a square bigger than the pipe end

materials.item: Galvanised wire, nylon string or glue to fix the screen; metal straps to fix the pipe
Boards, plywood or sheet for the cubicle walls, roof and door
Dark paint for the vent pipe

steps.text: Choose the site: at least 30 m from any well, spring, lake or stream, 40 m if you don't know the ground, and 50 m or more in sand or gravel (WEDC Guide 23, Compendium), on higher ground that doesn't flood, with the pit bottom well above the highest water table (see notes). Look at nearby wells and holes to judge the soil and water depth (WEDC Guide 24).
steps.warn: In cracked bedrock, no distance protects a well (WEDC Guide 23). Use a bucket or compost toilet there instead.

steps.text: Mark out a round pit 1 to 1.5 m across. Round pits hold their shape better than square ones (WEDC Guide 23, WEDC Guide 25).
Dig the top 0.5 to 1 m first, with a second person at the top the whole time. Slope loose sides back or prop them until the lining is in (WEDC Guide 24).
steps.warn: Pit walls can cave in and bury you (CCOHS trenching). Get out at once if one cracks or crumbles. Keep spoil at least 1 m back, and cover or fence the hole whenever you stop. In loose soil, don't dig deep: build a raised pit or two shallow pits (WEDC Guide 24).

steps.text: Line the top 0.5 to 1 m with blocks, brick or stone, mortared solid for at least the top 0.5 m and standing at least 10 cm above the ground (about 15 cm where the slab sits on it). Below that, leave some joints open so liquid can soak away, and line the whole pit if the soil is loose or you're unsure (WEDC Guide 24). Fill behind open linings with sand or gravel.

Dig the rest of the pit down inside the lining, with a second person at the top the whole time and a ladder in the hole. Don't stand in a pit deeper than 1.2 m (4 ft) unless its sides are sloped back, propped or cut in stable rock (CCOHS trenching). Aim for about 3 m deep where that is safe (WEDC Guide 25: at least 2 m, usually 2.5 to 4 m; Compendium: at least 3 m), and stop well above any water seeping in.
Make the slab from reinforced concrete or heavy timber, with a drop hole and a hole for the vent pipe. Test it with four people standing on it before use (WEDC Guide 25).
steps.warn: Wet cement burns skin and eyes. Wear gloves, goggles and long sleeves. Concrete that isn't cured properly for cold weather can be weak and collapse (WEDC Guide 29).

steps.text: Set the slab on the lining about 150 mm (6 in) above the ground, and mound soil around it so rain and melt run away from the pit (WEDC Guide 25).
steps.warn: A slab is heavy. Lift and slide it with two or more people, and never stand on the pit edge while doing it.

steps.text: Fit the vent pipe through its hole, straight and upright, sealed into the slab and strapped to the wall, with its top at least 0.5 m higher than the roof and any building nearby (WEDC Guide 27). Paint it dark so the sun warms it (WEDC Guide 27).
Sand the pipe's top edge smooth, then fix the fly screen over it with glue, galvanised wire or nylon string (WEDC Guide 27).
Build the cubicle dark inside, with a roof, a door and small screened air holes to let fresh air in, and the entrance facing the usual wind (WEDC Guide 27, TBDHU).
steps.warn: Work on the roof from a footed ladder, and cover the open pit while you build.

steps.text: Test it: hold a little smoke over the drop hole. It should be pulled down the hole and come out of the vent, not hang in the cubicle (Compendium).

Use it with the door shut and the drop hole open, so air keeps moving (WEDC Guide 27). Keep young children supervised, and put children's faeces in the latrine (WEDC Guide 25). Put a [tippy tap](#guides/build_tippy_tap) by the door.
Every 6 months or sooner, check the screen and clear cobwebs and dead flies, for example by pouring a bucket of water down the pipe. Check the pipe for cracks and loose fixings (WEDC Guide 27).
When winter comes, seal the vent pipe: in very cold months it pulls cold air through the pit (WEDC Guide 29). See [toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter).

When the waste is 0.5 m below the slab, the pit is full (WEDC Guide 23). Move the slab and cubicle to a new pit, fill the old one to the top with soil, mound it, and mark it or plant a tree on it (Compendium).
steps.warn: Never climb into a pit, even an old one or to rescue someone. Pits give off methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide (WEDC Guide 25), and sewage can make hydrogen sulphide, which numbs your sense of smell (WorkSafeBC H2S). The air can kill, rescuers included.

notes:
## How it works

- Wind blowing across the top of the vent pipe makes the air inside rise. Fresh air is drawn into the cubicle and down the drop hole, so the cubicle stays free of smells. With no wind, a sun-warmed pipe keeps the air moving (WEDC Guide 27).
- Flies head for light. In a dark cubicle, flies from the pit fly up the pipe towards the light, can't get past the screen, and die there (WEDC Guide 27).
- It works only if the cubicle is dark, the pipe is straight and screened, and the drop hole stays open (WEDC Guide 27).
- It doesn't stop mosquitoes. On cold, still mornings the air can flow the wrong way and bring smells into the cubicle (WEDC Guide 27).

## Where it can go

| Rule | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| From a drilled well (Ontario) | 15 m (50 ft) | TBDHU |
| From a dug well (Ontario) | 30 m (100 ft) | TBDHU |
| From a lake, river or stream (Ontario) | 15 m (50 ft) | TBDHU |
| From any water source (field guides) | 30 m | Compendium |
| Pit bottom above high water table or bedrock (Ontario) | 0.9 m (3 ft) | TBDHU |
| Pit bottom above water table (field guides) | 1.5 to 2 m | WEDC Guide 25, Compendium |

Use the larger figures where you can. How far germs travel depends on the ground (WEDC Guide 23):

| Ground between pit and well | Least distance |
|---|---|
| Silt | 10 m |
| Fine silty sand | 15 m |
| Medium sand | 50 m |
| Gravel | 500 m |
| Cracked (fractured) rock | No distance is enough |

If you don't know the ground, WEDC suggests 40 m from any water point (WEDC Guide 23). More in [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances).

- Avoid low, wet spots and swamps; open, high ground with air movement is best (TBDHU). Areas that flood often are unsuitable (Compendium).
- A VIP can stand close to the house if its pipe rises above the house roof (WEDC Guide 23). In cold country, closer is better: people avoid a long, cold walk (WEDC Guide 29).

## Sizing the pit

- Typical pits are 2.5 to 4 m deep and 1 to 1.5 m wide. A pit 3 m deep and 1.5 m square lasts a family of six about 15 years (WEDC Guide 25).
- A dry pit where people use paper fills at about 60 L a person a year; with things that don't rot, such as stones or sticks, it is about 90 L (WEDC Guide 23). Cold slows breakdown, so pits fill faster in cold regions (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Rough life (our own arithmetic from WEDC's figures, not a WEDC number):** litres of pit below the top 0.5 m ÷ (people × litres each a year). A round pit 1.2 m wide inside any lining and 3 m deep holds about 2,800 L below that line. With 60 L each (a dry pit, paper only, nothing else tipped in) that is about 12 years for 4 people; with 90 L each, about 8. Less in the cold. WEDC says pit life is not easy to estimate (WEDC Guide 23).

## Lining

The top 0.5 to 1 m is always lined, and at least the top 0.5 m is mortared into a solid ring. It carries the slab, keeps surface water out and stops rats and other burrowers getting in. Below that the lining is left porous so liquid soaks into the soil; many small holes are better than a few big ones, which let soil fall in (WEDC Guide 24).

| Usually needs lining all the way | Usually doesn't |
|---|---|
| Soft sand and gravel, loose soil, filled ground, compressed mudstone and shale | Soil with a lot of clay, strongly bonded sedimentary rock, iron-rich (laterite) soil |

Clay can change as it dries or as the water table rises and falls. If in doubt, line the whole pit (WEDC Guide 24).

- **Materials:** stone, fired brick, concrete or soil-cement blocks, or durable timber. Bamboo and cane only for pits used under 2 years (WEDC Guide 24).
- **Drums** are too weak alone; they need a concrete ring beam on top (WEDC Guide 24).
- **Sandbags** have lined pits in loose soil in camps in Kenya and Sudan, and proved cheaper, longer lasting and more stable than oil drums (WEDC Guide 24).
- **Foundations:** a pad about three times the lining's width under it in firm soil (WEDC Guide 24).

## Vent pipe and screen

| Part | WEDC Guide 27 | Compendium |
|---|---|---|
| Pipe inside size | 150 mm if smooth plastic; 200–250 mm if rough; 200 mm brick or home-made | At least 110 mm |
| Pipe height | At least 0.5 m above nearby buildings | More than 300 mm above the cubicle roof |
| Screen | 1.5 × 1.2 mm mesh; PVC-coated glass fibre lasts over 5 years | Aluminium, 1.2–1.5 mm holes |

Where they differ, build to the larger figure: WEDC's pipe size, and a top at least 0.5 m above the roof and any building nearby.

- Bigger holes let flies through; smaller ones choke the air flow. Cheap screens rust or get torn by birds and animals (WEDC Guide 27).
- Plastic pipe should have UV stabiliser, or sunlight weakens it (WEDC Guide 27).

## Children

- Children can be scared of a dark cubicle, and they leave doors open, which spoils the fly trap. A spiral entrance keeps the inside dark even with no door, and a half door can be added for privacy (WEDC Guide 27).
- A lid over the hole stops small children falling in on a simple pit (WEDC Guide 25). A VIP's hole has to stay open for the air to flow (WEDC Guide 27), so supervise young children.
- Ontario's guide suggests a second, lower bench for children and smaller people (TBDHU).
- Children's faeces are very infectious: put them in the latrine, and everyone washes with soap afterwards (WEDC Guide 25). Put a [tippy tap](#guides/build_tippy_tap) by the door.

## In winter

VIP latrines don't suit very cold months: the vent circulates cold air through the pit. Seal the pipe as the cold sets in, raise the slab to leave room for a frozen pile, and dig new pits before freeze-up. A pit dug into frozen ground can collapse as it thaws (WEDC Guide 29). The rest is in [toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter).

## Closing a full pit

A pit counts as full when the waste is 0.5 m below the slab. That last 0.5 m of soil makes the spot safe to walk over, stops animals digging in for food and keeps fly larvae from getting out (WEDC Guide 23). Filling and covering a full pit carries little risk if it is properly covered and clearly marked, but the contents can still reach groundwater until they have broken down (Compendium). A tree planted on top uses the nutrients and stops people falling into old pits (Compendium).

Never climb into a pit to dig it out, fetch something or rescue someone: see [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space). If a pit must be emptied instead, it is dirty, risky work: gloves, boots, overalls and a face mask at the least (Compendium), and always from outside the pit.
